About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Te Reo Māori Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Te Reo Māori Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Te Reo Māori Years 11–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Te Reo Māori Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Students use and apply this knowledge as they listen, speak, read, write, and interact

Te Reo Māori provides students with foundational knowledge and practices in
language learning. This includes the explicit teaching of pronunciation and
orthography, the formation and use of words, phrases, sentences, and connected
language, as well as culturally grounded language choices and expressions. Students
also learn about the whakapapa and reclamation of te reo Māori. Foundational
knowledge, such as pronunciation, stress patterns, and language structure, is
introduced early and progressively strengthened throughout the programme. As this
knowledge grows, students use te reo Māori with increasing accuracy, confidence,
and flexibility to express themselves, interact with others, engage with more complex
ideas and contexts, and contribute to the ongoing strength, vitality, and revitalisation
of te reo Māori.

Responsible use of AI

Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative
processes, but its use must uphold mana, tikanga, whakapapa, and tino
rangatiratanga. AI is not a neutral source of knowledge and may reproduce bias,
inaccuracies, or understandings inconsistent with mātauranga Māori or the
knowledge and values of whānau, hapū, and iwi. Māori knowledge, cultural practices,
narratives, language, and intellectual and cultural property must be protected from
inappropriate collection, use, interpretation, or reproduction.

Responsible use of AI requires students and teachers to exercise critical judgement
and discernment, considering where knowledge comes from, whose perspectives are
represented, and whose knowledge may be absent or misrepresented. AI should
support, not replace, mokopuna thinking, learning, creativity, relationships, and
decision-making. Where Māori knowledge is used, appropriate permissions,
relationships, attribution, and tikanga must be respected. AI-generated information
should be transparently identified and verified against trusted and appropriate
sources, including mātauranga Māori and the knowledge of whānau, hapū, and iwi.
